detail:
Mayo Clinic describes psoriatic arthritis treatment as aiming to manage symptoms, lessen inflammation, and protect joints and skin from damage, with the plan depending on severity and which joints are affected. Foundations in the sources include regular movement and exercise to maintain function, physical and occupational therapy to lessen pain and make daily activities easier, joint protection strategies, and skin care for the psoriasis itself, alongside regular follow-up to watch joint damage and medicine safety.

Medication classes clinicians may use include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain and swelling, conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as methotrexate that slow the disease, biologic DMARDs that target specific immune signals such as tumor necrosis factor and interleukin pathways, and other targeted oral medicines. Corticosteroid injections into a swollen joint are described for short-term relief, and joint replacement surgery only when a joint is severely damaged. Mayo Clinic notes there is no cure, so ongoing monitoring of joints, skin, and lab tests guides adjustments over time.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about psoriatic arthritis treatment options.
sourceVideoTitle: Psoriatic arthritis - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic
summary: Mayo Clinic describes psoriatic arthritis treatment built on therapy and movement to protect function, plus medication classes from NSAIDs to conventional and biologic DMARDs, chosen by severity and the joints involved.
takeaways: exercise and therapy help protect joint function
dmards aim to slow disease and prevent joint damage
regular follow-up watches joints, skin, and lab safety
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
title: Managing psoriatic arthritis day to day
